anchorCharts.name: Author's Purpose
anchorCharts.body: Authors write for a reason. Remember P.I.E.: to Persuade, to Inform, or to Entertain. Some texts also Explain how to do something. Ask: Why did the author write this? Look at the clues: facts and dates usually inform, characters and events usually entertain, and opinions with strong words usually persuade.
ex: A passage full of facts about Alexander Graham Bell's inventions is written to inform.
A funny story about a bunny and a lizard going fishing is written to entertain.
"Don't be discouraged by setbacks" and "remember the power of perseverance" are written to persuade or encourage.

anchorCharts.name: Text Structure
anchorCharts.body: Text structure is how the author organizes ideas. Five common structures: Description (tells about a topic with details), Sequence (events in order: first, next, then, finally), Cause and Effect (why something happened and what happened because of it: because, so, as a result, causing), Compare and Contrast (alike and different: both, however, unlike), and Problem and Solution (a problem and how it is fixed).
ex: "Benny's hops were too fast for Larry" (cause) → "Larry went tumbling head over tail" (effect).
Molly started at 6, then convinced her school, then spoke to the city council: sequence.
The crew lost fresh water (problem), so the captain collected rainwater (solution).

anchorCharts.name: Figurative Language
anchorCharts.body: Figurative language says something in a creative way that is not literally true. Simile compares with like or as. Metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human actions to non-human things. Idiom is a phrase whose meaning is different from the words (head over heels, a piece of cake). Hyperbole is a big exaggeration.
ex: "Larry went tumbling head over tail" is an idiom that means Larry fell upside down.
"The air was rich with the scent of salt and adventure": you cannot really smell adventure, so it is figurative.
"Her laugh was as loud as a school bell" is a simile.

anchorCharts.name: Central Idea
anchorCharts.body: The central idea is the most important point the author makes about the topic. Supporting details are the facts, examples, and reasons that prove it. To find it, ask: What is this mostly about? What do most of the details point to? A good central idea is not too narrow (one detail) and not too broad (the whole topic). The theme is different: it is the life lesson in a story.
ex: Central idea: Alexander Graham Bell was an inventor of many useful things. Detail: He created an early metal detector.
Central idea of the Molly passage: Molly's actions inspired others and made a big difference.
Theme of Benny and Larry: Having fun with friends matters more than success.

anchorCharts.name: Point of View
anchorCharts.body: Who is telling the story? First-person: the narrator is a character and uses I, me, we, us. Third-person: the narrator is outside the story and uses he, she, they. Third-person limited: the narrator knows and shares the thoughts of only one character. Third-person omniscient: the narrator knows everything and shares the thoughts of all characters, even things the characters do not know.
ex: "The dew on the grass made my running shoes damp. It didn't bother me." → first-person.
"Jeremiah squinted from the sun. He was thinking about the game." (only Jeremiah's thoughts) → third-person limited.
"Sarah didn't know that her teacher was also worried." (both characters' thoughts) → third-person omniscient.

passages.title: Alexander Graham Bell
passages.body:
From M1W1 HW3, Part A.

Alexander Graham Bell is most famous for inventing the telephone, but he also did much more in science and technology. He created one of the earliest versions of a metal detector, and he also had a great idea about heating homes with solar panels. The reason he became interested in making telephones was because his mother and wife were deaf (unable to hear), and he was also a teacher for deaf people. The invention of the telephone was one of the most important inventions for people then and now.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: Alexander Graham Bell's wife and mother were deaf.
Alexander Graham Bell was an inventor of many useful things.
Alexander Graham Bell had a great idea about solar panels.
Alexander Graham Bell was a teacher for deaf people.

questions.q: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Bell cared about people who could not hear?
choices: "He created one of the earliest versions of a metal detector."
"The reason he became interested in making telephones was because his mother and wife were deaf."
"He also had a great idea about heating homes with solar panels."
"The invention of the telephone was one of the most important inventions."

questions.q: The passage says Bell's mother and wife were "deaf (unable to hear)". The words in parentheses are an example of which kind of context clue?
choices: A definition clue that explains the word right after it
An antonym clue that gives the opposite
An example clue that lists examples
A comparison clue that uses like or as

questions.q: Which detail best supports the central idea that Bell invented many useful things?
choices: His mother and wife were deaf.
He created one of the earliest versions of a metal detector.
He was a teacher.
People use telephones now.

questions.q: Why did Bell become interested in making telephones?
choices: He wanted to become rich and famous.
His mother and wife were deaf, and he taught deaf people.
He needed a way to find metal.
His house was too cold in winter.

questions.q: The author's purpose in this passage is mostly to ____.
choices: entertain readers with a funny story
persuade readers to buy a telephone
inform readers about Bell's inventions and life
explain how to build a metal detector

questions.q: Name one invention that has changed the world. Explain why.
questions.sampleAnswer: The internet has changed the world because it lets people communicate and share information quickly across long distances.

passages.title: The Super-Recycler
passages.body:
From M1W1 HW3, Part B.

1 We all know that recycling is important for the environment. But for Molly, a 10-year-old girl, recycling is more than just a good habit—it's a mission. Molly started recycling when she was only 6 years old. She began by collecting aluminum cans and plastic bottles from her neighborhood.

2 Molly didn't just stop at her neighborhood. She convinced her school to start a recycling program, and even gave presentations at city council meetings. She explained how recycling could help the environment and also save money. She used her own pocket money to buy recycling bins for her school.

3 She set up recycling centers in her local park and at community events. Molly even created a YouTube channel where she teaches people how to recycle effectively. Her efforts have resulted in her town recycling 40% more waste than before.

4 One day, a documentary team decided to make a film about her. The film, called "The Super-Recycler", won several awards and helped to spread Molly's message even further. Thanks to Molly, more people are now conscious of the importance of recycling.

5 Molly says, "It's not just about saving the planet for future generations. It's about making the world a better place right now."

questions.q: Which of these best shows how Molly's work had a real impact, or big change, on her community?
choices: She started recycling when she was 6 years old.
She made a YouTube channel about recycling.
Her town now recycles 40% more waste than before.
A documentary was made about her story.

questions.q: Which statement would fit best as the missing central idea of Paragraph 3?
choices: Molly was only 10 years old when she started her mission.
Molly's school was resistant to starting a recycling program.
Molly took her mission beyond her school and neighborhood.
Molly's family was very supportive of her recycling efforts.

questions.q: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that Molly used her own money for her mission?
choices: "She began by collecting aluminum cans and plastic bottles from her neighborhood."
"She used her own pocket money to buy recycling bins for her school."
"Molly even created a YouTube channel where she teaches people how to recycle effectively."
"The film, called 'The Super-Recycler', won several awards."

questions.q: In paragraph 4, "more people are now conscious of the importance of recycling." What does conscious mean here?
choices: aware; knowing about something
asleep
angry
afraid

questions.q: Paragraph 1 says recycling is "more than just a good habit—it's a mission." What does the author want readers to understand about Molly?
choices: Recycling is something she does only when she remembers.
Recycling is a serious, important goal that she works hard for.
Recycling is a job she is paid for.
Recycling is a hobby she does on weekends.

questions.q: How does the author organize paragraphs 1 to 4?
choices: In the order the events happened, from age 6 until now
By comparing Molly with other recyclers
By listing problems with no solutions
By describing what a recycling bin looks like

questions.q: This passage is told from which point of view?
choices: First-person, by Molly
Third-person, by a narrator outside the story
First-person, by the documentary team
Second-person, talking to you

questions.q: What is the central idea of the entire passage about Molly?
questions.sampleAnswer: Molly's actions inspired other people and made a big difference in how much her community recycles.

passages.title: The Power of Perseverance
passages.body:
From M1W2 HW3, Part B.

Perseverance is a quality that can change your life. It means not giving up when faced with challenges and obstacles, and it's a crucial skill to develop as you grow older.

Consider the story of Abraham Lincoln. He faced numerous failures and setbacks throughout his life. He lost multiple elections and even went bankrupt, but he didn't give up. He continued to work hard, learn from his mistakes, and, eventually, became one of the greatest presidents in American history.

Another example is the story of J.K. Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series. She received rejection letters from numerous publishers before one finally accepted her manuscript. Today, her books have sold millions of copies worldwide, and she's a household name.

Inventor Thomas Edison once said, "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work." His determination led to the invention of the light bulb, which revolutionized the world.

Perseverance isn't just about achieving big dreams; it's also about tackling everyday challenges. Whether it's a tough math problem, a difficult friendship, or a new skill you're trying to master, remember that you can overcome anything with determination and hard work.

So, as you journey through life, keep in mind the power of perseverance. Don't be discouraged by setbacks, and remember that some of the world's greatest achievements were made possible by those who refused to give up.

questions.q: What is the central idea of the passage?
choices: the significance of famous inventors in history
the challenges of becoming a successful author
the power of perseverance in overcoming obstacles
the importance of learning from mistakes

questions.q: Which famous inventor's quote is mentioned in the passage as an example of perseverance?
choices: Abraham Lincoln
J.K. Rowling
Thomas Edison

questions.q: Which of the following is the opposite of perseverance?
choices: determination
giving up

questions.q: Which sentence from the passage best supports the idea that perseverance matters in everyday life, not only for famous people?
choices: "He lost multiple elections and even went bankrupt, but he didn't give up."
"Today, her books have sold millions of copies worldwide."
"Whether it's a tough math problem, a difficult friendship, or a new skill you're trying to master, remember that you can overcome anything."
"His determination led to the invention of the light bulb."

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "she's a household name." What does this phrase mean?
choices: She is famous; almost everyone knows her name.
She works at home.
Her name is written on her house.
She only sells books to families.

questions.q: What reason does the author give to support the point that Abraham Lincoln showed perseverance?
choices: He wrote many books.
He lost elections and went bankrupt but kept working hard.
He invented the light bulb.
He was born in a log cabin.

questions.q: Why does the author include the stories of Lincoln, Rowling, and Edison?
choices: To give examples that support the central idea
To compare which person was the smartest
To explain how to write a book
To show that famous people never fail

questions.q: The author's purpose in the last two paragraphs is mostly to ____.
choices: inform readers about the history of the light bulb
persuade readers to keep trying and not give up
entertain readers with a funny story

questions.q: What did Thomas Edison mean when he said, "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways that won't work"?
questions.sampleAnswer: He meant that each mistake taught him something, so his failures were really steps toward success and he refused to give up.

passages.title: Benny and Larry
passages.body:
From M1W3 HW3, Part A.

One sunny morning, Benny was hopping through the meadow when he spotted his friend Larry sunbathing on a rock. Benny, being the curious bunny that he was, hopped over to say hello. Larry, a lizard with a cool and laid-back personality, welcomed Benny's company. Since neither Benny nor Larry had plans for the day, the two decided to spend some time together.

First, Benny invited Larry to hop along with him through the carrot patch. Benny's nimble hops turned out to be too fast for Larry's wobbly waddle. Larry went tumbling head over tail, causing the carrots to fly in all directions. Oops!

After that, Benny and Larry decided to go fishing. Benny thought that if he hopped around the pond, he could create ripples that would attract the fish. Larry, not wanting to be left out, joined in by flicking his tail into the water. The combination of Benny's hops and Larry's tail flicks created such chaos that the fish swam away in a frenzy. Benny and Larry ended up with a bucket of water, but no fish!

In the end, it was clear that Benny the bunny and Larry the lizard didn't always have the best ideas, but they always managed to have a fun time. And that, my friends, is what made them the most beloved and entertaining duo in the entire village.

questions.q: What does the phrase "head over tail" mean in the story?
choices: Larry was very happy.
Larry fell upside down.
Benny jumped very high.
Larry was chasing Benny.

questions.q: What is the theme, or main subject or topic, of this passage?
choices: Friends always win.
Having fun is more important than success.
Find friends that have different interests.
Exercise is important for your health.

questions.q: How are Benny and Larry different?
choices: Benny is quick and curious, while Larry is slow and laid-back.
Benny is lazy, while Larry is energetic.
Benny lives in the pond, while Larry lives in the meadow.
Benny is a lizard, while Larry is a bunny.

questions.q: Which sentence from the story best shows that the two friends are alike in one way?
choices: "Larry, a lizard with a cool and laid-back personality, welcomed Benny's company."
"Since neither Benny nor Larry had plans for the day, the two decided to spend some time together."
"Benny's nimble hops turned out to be too fast for Larry's wobbly waddle."
"Benny and Larry ended up with a bucket of water, but no fish!"

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "the fish swam away in a frenzy." What does frenzy mean?
choices: a wild, excited rush
a slow, calm way
a straight line
a deep sleep

questions.q: What caused the fish to swim away in a frenzy?
choices: Larry fell into the pond.
Benny's hops and Larry's tail flicks created chaos in the water.
The carrots flew into the pond.
A bucket fell into the water.

questions.q: Which words signal cause and effect in "Larry went tumbling head over tail, causing the carrots to fly in all directions"?
choices: causing
tumbling
in all directions
head over tail

questions.q: The narrator tells what Benny thought AND what Larry wanted. This story is told in ____.
choices: first-person
third-person limited
third-person omniscient
second-person

questions.q: Give one example of cause-and-effect in the passage.
questions.sampleAnswer: Cause: Benny's nimble hops were too fast for Larry's wobbly waddle. Effect: Larry went tumbling head over tail, causing the carrots to fly in all directions.

passages.title: Captain Morgan
passages.body:
From M1W3 HW3, Part B.

Captain Morgan stood at the helm of his ship, The Sea Whisperer, as it glided through the choppy waters. With a sparkle in his eye and a determined smile, he took a deep breath; the air was rich with the scent of salt and adventure. The crew admired Captain Morgan, not just for his skill in navigating treacherous waters but for the kind of person he was.

One day, a young sailor accidentally knocked over a barrel of fresh water. Everyone knew how important fresh water was on a long journey. But instead of getting angry, Captain Morgan calmly said, "Mistakes happen to the best of us. Let's find a way to collect rainwater to make up for the loss."

The crew was relieved and immediately got to work, inspired by their captain's character.

choices: impatient
understanding
eccentric
indifferent

choices: "Captain Morgan stood at the helm of his ship, The Sea Whisperer."
"The crew admired Captain Morgan, not just for his skill in navigating treacherous waters but for the kind of person he was."
"One day, a young sailor accidentally knocked over a barrel of fresh water."
"Everyone knew how important fresh water was on a long journey."

choices: dangerous
calm

choices: excited and happy
crying
wearing glasses

choices: Because the sea does not smell like salt
Because you cannot really smell adventure; it describes a feeling

choices: The crew felt relieved and got to work.

choices: inform readers about how ships collect rainwater
persuade readers to become sailors
entertain readers with a story that shows what a kind leader is like

questions.sampleAnswer: He is a kind and understanding person. Instead of getting angry when the sailor spilled the water, he calmly said, "Mistakes happen to the best of us," and found a solution.

passages.title: Point of View Practice
passages.body: From M1W2 HW3, Part A. Read each excerpt and decide who is telling the story. First-person: the narrator is in the story and uses I, me, we, us. Third-person limited: the narrator is outside the story (he, she, they) and shares the thoughts of only ONE character. Third-person omniscient: the narrator knows everything and shares the thoughts of ALL characters, even things the characters do not know. Excerpt 1. Red looked across the prairie. He didn't see anything concerning. He wondered why Texas Joe had hollered like that. Texas Joe turned to him. The ghost that Texas Joe had just seen was gone. Texas Joe swatted at the air. Now he felt crazy. Excerpt 2. The dew on the grass made my running shoes damp. It didn't bother me. The sound of my feet hitting the street formed a rhythm, a steady pattern of light thumps. I timed my breathing with the rhythm. These sounds filled my head. Excerpt 3. Jeremiah squinted from the sun. He was thinking about the game. They could have won. He could have won the game for them. All he needed to do was catch the ball, but he didn't. Excerpt 4. I couldn't believe what I was seeing. The recycling bin was overflowing, and nobody seemed to care. I knew I had to do something about this problem in my school. Excerpt 5. Tom picked up the plastic bottle from the ground. He wondered if one person could really make a difference in saving the environment. The other students watched him curiously. Excerpt 6. Sarah walked into the classroom feeling nervous. She didn't know that her teacher, Mrs. Johnson, was also worried about the upcoming presentation. Both of them were thinking about how the other students would react. Excerpt 7. Lily stared at the broken gadget on her desk. She was sure she could fix it before her brother came home. She did not want him to find out. Excerpt 8. We pushed the wheelchair up the ramp together. My arms were tired, but I was not going to stop now. This was our race.

passages.title: Schools Should Fund Young Inventors
passages.body:
An opinion text. The author gives an opinion and supports it with reasons and evidence, like "Government Must Fund Inventors" in Into Reading.

1 Every year, students at our school come up with clever ideas: a backpack that charges a phone, a bird feeder that scares away squirrels, a gadget that reminds you to drink water. Most of these ideas never get built. The reason is simple. Building a prototype costs money, and most ten-year-olds do not have it. I believe schools should set aside money every year to fund student inventors.

2 First, funding young inventors teaches skills that last a lifetime. When a student builds a prototype, she does not just follow directions. She must plan, measure, test, fail, and try again. A survey of 120 students at Maple Hill Elementary found that students who finished an invention project were twice as likely to say they enjoyed problem-solving. Those are exactly the habits that employers look for, and they cannot be learned from a worksheet.

3 Second, small amounts of money make a big difference. Most student inventions need only cheap materials: cardboard, wire, batteries, a used motor. At Riverside School, the parent club gave each inventor a budget of just $15. With that money, one fifth grader built a locomotive-shaped toy that teaches younger children to count. The school spent less on the whole program than it spends on one field trip.

4 Some people argue that schools have more important things to pay for, such as books and computers. That is true, but funding inventors does not have to replace those things. A school could hold a bake sale, ask local businesses for help, or use money from the science budget. Others say that most student inventions are flops. They are right, too. Thomas Edison's first inventions were flops as well. Failure is not a reason to stop; it is part of how inventing works.

5 Finally, funding inventors sends a message. It tells students that their ideas matter and that the school is passionate about learning, not only about test scores. When Riverside School displayed its student inventions in the auditorium, attendance at the science fair doubled the next year.

6 Great ideas should not depend on how much money a family has. If schools fund young inventors, they will build better problem-solvers, better students, and maybe the next great invention. The objective is not to make every student an inventor. It is to make sure that the ones who could be are never stopped by the price of a battery.

choices: "Most of these ideas never get built."

choices: having very strong feelings about something

choices: entertain readers with a story about a toy locomotive

passages.title: Rolling into the Game
passages.body:
An informational text about wheelchair sports.

1 The whistle blows, and ten players race down the court. Wheels squeal on the wooden floor as a player spins, blocks, and fires a pass across the key. This is wheelchair basketball, one of the fastest and most popular wheelchair sports in the world.

2 Wheelchair sports began in the 1940s, after the Second World War. Many soldiers came home with injuries that meant they could no longer walk. A doctor in England named Ludwig Guttmann believed that sports could help these veterans grow stronger in body and in spirit. In 1948, he organized a small competition for wheelchair athletes on the same day the Olympic Games opened in London. That small event grew into the Paralympic Games, which today bring together thousands of athletes from around the world.

3 Wheelchair basketball follows most of the same rules as regular basketball. The court is the same size, and the hoop is the same height. But there is one important difference. Instead of dribbling every step, a player may push the wheels twice and then must dribble, pass, or shoot. Pushing three times without dribbling is called traveling, just like walking with the ball in the regular game.

4 The chairs themselves are built for the sport. A sports wheelchair is light and strong, with wheels that tilt outward at the bottom. This tilt, called camber, lets a player turn quickly and keeps the chair from tipping over when two players bump. A small wheel at the back stops the chair from flipping backward during a hard push. Players learn to maneuver their chairs so well that they can stop, spin, and change direction in a single second.

5 Many other sports have wheelchair versions, too. Wheelchair racing uses long, three-wheeled chairs built for acceleration on the track. Wheelchair tennis allows the ball to bounce twice instead of once. Wheelchair rugby, sometimes called "murderball," is played with a volleyball on a basketball court, and chairs crash into each other on purpose.

6 Wheelchair athletes train as hard as any other athletes. They lift weights, practice for hours, and study game films. Elite players travel to compete in leagues and world championships. As one coach put it, "The chair is just equipment, like a bat or a pair of skates. The athlete is the one who wins the game."

choices: Wheelchair basketball has a hoop that is the same height as in regular basketball.
Wheelchair sports are real, fast, competitive sports with their own history and equipment.

Wheelchair rugby is sometimes called murderball.

choices: It compares two sports.

choices: "Wheels squeal on the wooden floor as a player spins."
"A small wheel at the back stops the chair from flipping backward during a hard push."
"Wheelchair tennis allows the ball to bounce twice instead of once."

choices: By giving a definition right in the sentence
By giving an antonym

choices: To explain how to build a wheelchair

To describe a game film

questions.q: What effect did Ludwig Guttmann's 1948 competition have?
choices: It grew into the Paralympic Games.
It ended the Second World War.
It changed the height of the hoop.
It made wheelchair rugby popular.

questions.q: The author's purpose in this passage is mostly to ____.
choices: persuade readers to try out for a team
inform readers about wheelchair sports
entertain readers with a made-up story
explain how to fix a broken wheel

questions.q: Use two details from the passage to explain how a sports wheelchair is different from an everyday wheelchair.
questions.sampleAnswer: A sports wheelchair is light and strong, its wheels tilt outward (camber) so it turns fast without tipping, and it has a small back wheel that stops it from flipping backward.

passages.title: The Flying Bathtub
passages.body:
A story. Notice whose thoughts the narrator shares.

1 Everyone in Pebble Harbor knew Uncle Rafael was eccentric. He wore a fishing hat in the bathtub and a bathing cap to go fishing. He kept a phonograph on his porch and played marching songs to his tomatoes. But Mara, who was ten and spent every summer at his house, thought he was the most interesting person she had ever met.

2 That June, Uncle Rafael announced that he was going to fly. Not in an airplane. In a bathtub. "Every great inventor starts with something people laugh at," he said, tapping a drawing pinned to the kitchen wall. The drawing showed an old iron tub with two bicycle wheels, a sail made from a bedsheet, and a propeller from a broken fan.

3 Mara's stomach did a small flip. She had heard the neighbors whisper about Uncle Rafael's "flops": the self-stirring soup pot that painted the ceiling, the alarm clock that rang only on holidays. She did not want to see him laughed at again. But she picked up a wrench anyway, because that was what you did for family.

4 For three weeks they worked in the barn. The tub sputtered and groaned every time they tested the motor. Mara measured. Uncle Rafael hummed. When the propeller finally spun without smoking, he danced around the barn like a puppet with tangled strings.

5 On the morning of the test, half the town lined the hill above the harbor. Mara heard Mr. Duffy say, "Ten dollars says it doesn't leave the ground." Her cheeks burned. She wanted to shout at him, but she stayed by the tub and checked the ropes one more time.

6 Uncle Rafael climbed in, pulled his fishing hat down tight, and gave her a thumbs-up. The tub rolled down the hill, slowly at first, then faster. The bedsheet snapped full of wind. For one long second, the front wheels lifted. The tub floated, wobbled, and came down with a tremendous splash in the shallow water at the bottom of the hill.

7 The crowd was silent. Then Mr. Duffy began to laugh, and Mara felt her face grow hot again. But Uncle Rafael stood up in the tub, dripping and grinning, and raised both arms. "One second!" he shouted. "It flew for one whole second!"

8 Walking home, Mara was quiet. Finally she asked, "Doesn't it bother you when they laugh?" Uncle Rafael thought about it. "They laughed at the first bicycle, too," he said. "The trick is to be so busy building the next one that you don't have time to listen." Mara looked at the wet drawing in his hand. He had already sketched a second propeller.

questions.q: From whose point of view is the story told?
choices: First-person, told by Mara
First-person, told by Uncle Rafael
Third-person limited, sharing only Mara's thoughts and feelings
Third-person omniscient, sharing everyone's thoughts

questions.q: Which sentence from the story best shows that the narrator shares Mara's feelings but not Mr. Duffy's?
choices: "Everyone in Pebble Harbor knew Uncle Rafael was eccentric."
"Her cheeks burned. She wanted to shout at him, but she stayed by the tub."
"The tub rolled down the hill, slowly at first, then faster."
"He had already sketched a second propeller."

questions.q: "He danced around the barn like a puppet with tangled strings." This is an example of ____.
choices: a simile that shows his wild, happy movements
a metaphor that says he is a puppet
personification of the barn
hyperbole about the barn's size

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "Mara's stomach did a small flip." What does this tell the reader?
choices: Mara was nervous and worried.
Mara was hungry.
Mara had been doing gymnastics.
Mara was angry at her uncle.

questions.q: Which word best describes Uncle Rafael?
choices: easily discouraged
persistent
careless with his family
shy

questions.q: How does Mara change from paragraph 3 to paragraph 8?
choices: She stops caring about her uncle.
She moves from worrying about people laughing to understanding why her uncle keeps going.
She decides to bet with Mr. Duffy.
She learns to fly the bathtub herself.

questions.q: Which theme does the story best support?
choices: Never try anything that might fail.
Keep working on your ideas even when people laugh.
Bathtubs are not meant to fly.
Family members should not help each other.

questions.q: In paragraph 1, the neighbors call Uncle Rafael eccentric. Which detail from the paragraph is the best clue to what eccentric means?
choices: He lived in Pebble Harbor.
He wore a fishing hat in the bathtub and a bathing cap to go fishing.
Mara was ten years old.
Mara spent every summer at his house.

questions.q: What caused the tub to lift off the ground for one second?
choices: Mr. Duffy pushed it.
The bedsheet sail filled with wind as the tub sped down the hill.
The marching songs on the phonograph
The crowd cheered loudly.

questions.q: Why does Uncle Rafael mention the first bicycle in paragraph 8? Use a detail from the story in your answer.
questions.sampleAnswer: He mentions the first bicycle because people laughed at it too, and it still changed the world. He wants Mara to understand that being laughed at does not mean an idea is bad, which is why he has already sketched a second propeller.

passages.imageAlt: Mara watches Uncle Rafael test his bathtub with bicycle wheels, a bedsheet sail and a propeller.
